anchor.context: I added the study by \citet{mccrea_disynaptic_1995} to SADb. The authors stimulated the plantaris nerve and recorded from motor neurons supplying another ankle extensor, the medial gastrocnemius. They compared the response at rest and during extension in immobilized cats. Midbrain stimulation evoked the neural rhythm of stepping without leg movement, a pattern of neural activity called fictive locomotion (Section~\ref{sec:bg_sensory}). The nerve stimulus recruited group~I afferents from muscle spindles (Ia) and tendon organs (Ib).

anchor.text: who wishes to implement this pathways
anchor.context: The response constrains what a controller must reproduce. The same input to the same motor pool must have opposite net effects at rest and during extension (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_group_i_rule}). A separate tendon-stretch experiment isolated an excitatory contribution from Ia fibers (Figure~4 of \citet{mccrea_disynaptic_1995}). The authors included Ib input in their proposed circuit (their Figure~8), but did not stimulate Ib fibers alone. A modeler who wishes to implement this pathways must still choose the interneurons, gains, and delays in a circuit such as those in Figures~\ref{fig:rybak_cpg_circuit} and~\ref{fig:afferent_connectomes}. Appendix~\ref{app:sadb_records} compares these results with those from cats whose spinal cords had been transected.

anchor.context: MyoConverter is a (open-source?) program that translates OpenSim muscle paths and joint geometry into a model for MuJoCo \citep{caggiano_myosuite_2022,wang_myosim_2022}. I used it to convert the human reference, \path{gait2392_simbody.osim}, restored missing maximum-force scales from the OpenSim source, and checked the direction of each tested muscle's joint action. The model retains 92 actuator entries, including six disabled small hip rotators, and the OpenSim convention of negative knee flexion. Moving the joints through their ranges exposed changes in moment arm at moving points and wrap surfaces. A separate check verified that foot contact produced ground forces (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_conversion_repairs}).

anchor.context: I next developed \path{gait2392_robotbody.osim}, which contains the muscle routes proposed for the robot. In my earlier design I had moved actuator origins, insertions, and via points to respect the usable BPA contraction and avoid interference \citep{bolen_bipedal_2019,morrow_optimization_2020}. My preparation script mirrored the intended right-side routes to the left and wrote \path{gait2392_robot.osim} for conversion. Applying human muscle parameters to the new paths caused equilibrium failures because the routed lengths had changed. With converted Hill-type actuators, the legs of the suspended robot model made repeated stepping-like movements. To test a BPA on the same geometry, I supplied a separate force law.
